data.topic: The full story behind a prospector's horrifying 1874 ordeal in Colorado's San Juan Mountains — what really happened, beyond what this video tells

read.lede: Alfred Packer’s 1874 ordeal has two incompatible centers: a starving guide who says he found his companions dead and ate them to survive, and a known liar who may have led five men into the mountains, killed them, taken their money, and invented the cannibalism story afterward. The surviving evidence never cleanly resolves which version is true. The reconstruction and its uncertainties rest on a single narrated account, not independent confirmations. Packer had served briefly in the Union Army during the Civil War, but epilepsy and seizures led to two honorable discharges; later, his work as a guide, hunter, range hand, animal driver, miner, and mining-company laborer repeatedly ended because of his temper, dishonesty, or incompetence.

paragraphs.label: Arrival and suspicion
paragraphs.text: On April 16, 1874, Packer staggered into the Los Piños Indian Agency near Saguache during a fierce snowstorm, wearing rags instead of shoes, carrying a rifle and coffee pot, and begging for help. General Charles Adams’s men led him to a table. He was starving enough to vomit after eating too quickly, but he did not look like the nearly skeletal survivors agency workers were accustomed to seeing. His bloated face, full-looking belly, unexplained cash, and possession of other men’s belongings immediately made people suspicious of his first story. Packer said that the five men who had traveled with him became too exhausted to continue, and that snow blindness and frostbite had forced him to fend for himself. He said he survived for months on rabbits, roots, and rosebuds. In Saguache, he rented a room at a saloon, spent more than $100 on drinking and gambling—about $3,800 in 2023—and another $78 at a general store, despite joining the expedition with no money and receiving only $10 for the rifle he sold at the agency. People noticed that he gave conflicting accounts, seemed to have a different wallet whenever he went out, and never seemed to run out of cash. The journey from Utah to Colorado had quickly become dangerous, and the travelers eventually split over whether to continue.

paragraphs.label: The expedition
paragraphs.text: It began on November 20, 1873, when roughly twenty fortune-seekers left Bingham Canyon, Utah, for the newly advertised Colorado goldfields near Breckenridge, where newspapers claimed anyone with sense could make a fortune. Packer joined them about twenty-five miles south of Salt Lake City after claiming to know the route between Utah and Colorado. He had worked briefly as a guide, but his record was poor: he often got lost, argued with clients, stole from people, lied, and repeatedly lost jobs because no one trusted him. The first 260 miles were slow and difficult. Heavy snow obscured the trail, the wagons could barely follow a path, and the travelers eventually lost their way. By January, they had run out of food and were eating horse feed while considering whether they would have to eat the horses. On January 21, near Montrose, Chief Ouray and a Ute band found them, fed them, and offered shelter until spring. Ouray warned that no Ute would attempt the crossing in those conditions and said it would mean certain death. The prospectors ignored him because they feared that other prospectors would reach the goldfields first. The party split: some men stayed with the horses and wagons, while the group that included Packer and five others attempted to reach the agency.

paragraphs.label: The route and the five missing men
paragraphs.text: Starvation and exposure were plausible, but the same conditions make Packer’s decision to lead the group over the mountains look exceptionally reckless. Ouray advised the travelers to descend to the Gunnison River, follow it, and then turn north toward the agency. Packer insisted that crossing the mountains directly would be faster because he supposedly knew the country, and five men believed him. The alternative party followed the river, ran out of food, and would have starved without cowhands, who provided food and shelter at their cattle camp until spring. Its four members reached the agency in May, while Packer had arrived earlier, alone. The leader of Packer’s party later said that the men initially followed the river on horseback until the horses could go no farther, after which he unloaded their provisions and returned the animals to Ouray’s camp. They appear to have continued along the river before taking a high mountain route. Their leader knew they lacked enough supplies for a winter crossing but turned back after exhausting himself arguing with Packer. They had roughly fourteen days of food—barely enough for one man for a week—along with inadequate clothing, no snowshoes or flints, very few matches, a few rifles, a pistol, a hatchet, and knives. The leader’s decision to leave them was therefore itself a warning: he knew they could not reach the agency, but had had enough of Packer’s arguments. After that, no one heard from the five men again until Packer appeared at the agency.

paragraphs.label: Changing stories
paragraphs.text: Packer’s account became a public case involving survival cannibalism, although Preston Nutter, the river party’s leader, remained convinced that Packer had killed the men and stolen their possessions. Nutter challenged Packer’s first explanation, and Packer changed it. Nutter said the men would not have abandoned Packer, identified the rifle Packer had sold as belonging to an older party member, and recognized Packer’s discarded pipe as Shannon Bell’s. A council began questioning Packer. Two Ute men then arrived with pieces of flesh they said came from a human found on a nearby hill. Packer reportedly panicked, fainted, begged for mercy, and gave a sworn account. Before doing so, he said, “It would not be the first time that people had been obliged to eat each other when they were hungry,” making survival cannibalism part of the public case. He said the oldest man died ten days into the journey, after which the survivors ate him and took his rifle. Five days later, another man died, and they found $133 in his pockets. A third man died while Packer was away gathering wood, and the remaining men ate him. Packer said Bell then shot the others, carried some of the bodies as food, and buried the rest. Two weeks later, Bell allegedly attacked Packer, forcing Packer to shoot him in self-defense. Nutter did not believe the story; the dispute became so heated that he dragged Packer outside and nearly killed him before others intervened. Packer was arrested for manslaughter and held in the sheriff’s log cabin. When General Adams later took him and others into the mountains to recover the bodies, they found nothing and returned him to his cell.

paragraphs.label: Bodies and forensic questions
paragraphs.text: Illustrator John Randolph found the bodies in August near a tributary of the Gunnison, close to the place Packer had identified as Bell’s death site. Randolph saw five bodies in different stages of decomposition, several with blunt-force injuries to the head. One was nearly bones, apparently exposed to animals; Bell had been stripped almost to the bones, leaving only his hands and feet. The remains indicated that edible portions had been deliberately removed rather than simply consumed by animals. A team of twenty volunteers later retrieved the bodies. A coroner concluded that blows to the head had killed all five while they slept, citing the absence of defensive wounds and the similar markings on their skulls. Rags beneath their feet suggested that the men had eaten the leather from their shoes. A track led to a makeshift shelter, raising the possibility that Packer killed the men for their possessions, became trapped by worsening weather, and then ate them to survive. Hunters later testified that game remained plentiful in the area, including rabbits and deer, weakening Packer’s claim that cannibalism had been unavoidable. The findings were expected to upgrade his charge to first-degree murder. Before that happened, however, someone slipped him a key, penknife, and food. He escaped and remained under a false name for nine years.

paragraphs.label: Packer’s final account
paragraphs.text: After Cheyenne authorities recaptured Packer on March 11, 1883, he offered a final story that he largely maintained until his death. He had been using the name John Schwartze and was recognized by a former fellow prospector at a Cheyenne supply shop. Packer said the party had food for only one man for a week, that a snowstorm struck within two or three days, and that they survived for about ten days on rosebuds and pine gum while climbing ridges to avoid deeper snow. At a frozen lake, possibly Lake San Cristobal, Bell supposedly became furious and unstable. Packer went scouting with a pistol and returned to find Bell eating a piece of meat beside one dead man and three other apparently dead men. When Bell attacked him with a hatchet, Packer shot him in the stomach and then finished him. Packer spent roughly two months—about sixty days—in a shelter, finally ate Bell’s meat, and gathered more from the bodies. An avalanche exposed yellow clay that told him he was near Slumgullion Pass, whose color reminded settlers of slumgullion stew. He admitted taking money from the men’s pockets and later acknowledged that, during an earlier search expedition, he had deliberately stopped General Adams from reaching the bodies because he could not face the scene again. He said he escaped because he feared a mob would kill him after Nutter had nearly done so. He went first to Arkansas, worked on a ranch under a false name, moved to Arizona, and eventually reached Cheyenne.

paragraphs.label: Trials and legacy
paragraphs.text: The prosecution treated Packer’s survival account as a cover story for deliberate murder. Witnesses said he had tried to learn how much money the travelers possessed, knowingly led them onto the more dangerous winter route, and behaved dishonestly after reaching Saguache. Packer’s own six-hour testimony hurt him because he admitted eating the men but insisted that Bell alone was responsible for the killings. A jury convicted him of premeditated murder, theft, and other charges and sentenced him to hang. The court overturned that conviction because Colorado had not yet been a state when the killings occurred: Colorado Territory lacked a murder statute applicable to the crime, and the state laws used against him came later. At a second trial, the food-abundance argument and the charge of reckless guidance persuaded the jury. Packer was convicted of voluntary manslaughter and sentenced to forty years, the maximum eight years per victim and, according to the account, the longest prison sentence then imposed in the United States. Reporter Polly Pry of the Denver Post later recast him as a persecuted ex-soldier and argued that anyone would have eaten human flesh under those conditions. Her campaign produced petitions and helped secure his parole in 1901, after eighteen years in prison. Afterward, Packer worked briefly as a Denver Post guard, was described as kind and charitable, bought a copper mine in Littleton, and returned to prospecting. He died in 1907 at sixty-five; rumors that he had become a vegetarian remain unverified.

paragraphs.label: What the evidence permits
paragraphs.text: Later forensic examinations generally leaned toward guilt. One group reported marks across Bell’s forearms consistent with defensive injuries, contrary to Packer’s claim that Bell was shot once and quickly finished. But a 1994 discovery complicates that conclusion. An 1862 Colt revolver found at the murder site still held three .38-caliber bullets, and those bullets matched lead fragments found in Bell’s hip. That match suggests that at least part of Packer’s account may be true. The evidence supports parts of both positions: Packer may have been a deliberate killer, but parts of his desperate-survivor account may also be true. The fight remains between the deliberate-killer and desperate-survivor interpretations. What is honestly missing is a definitive reconstruction of who inflicted the head injuries, a fully documented chain of forensic analysis, and an independent account that can test Packer’s changing stories against the surviving evidence.

record.what: The party that Packer eventually joined left Bingham Canyon, Utah, on November 20, 1873.
record.context: This departure began the winter journey that would later become central to the Packer story. Leaving in late November placed the group in the mountains during a particularly difficult season.

record.what: In 1874, six men entered Colorado’s San Juan Mountains in winter hoping to reach newly discovered goldfields on the other side.
record.context: The expedition was driven by the promise of gold, but its route required crossing the San Juan Mountains in winter. The decision put the men in a dangerous setting before they could reach the fields they sought.

record.what: On the morning of April 16, 1874, workers at Los Piños Indian Agency near Saguache, Colorado were eating breakfast when Alfred Packer appeared in the mess hall doorway during a snowstorm.
record.context: Packer’s unexpected arrival brought the mountain expedition into public view. Appearing at an agency during a snowstorm connected him to the missing prospectors and created the first immediate opportunity to learn what had happened.

record.what: Packer’s lawyers discovered that Colorado Territory had no murder statute before Colorado became a state in 1876.
record.context: The legal discovery gave Packer’s defense a technical argument against a murder conviction. It also tied the case to Colorado’s changing legal status and the transition from territorial government to statehood.

record.what: In 1883, one of the original prospectors who had stayed with Chief Ouray opened a supply shop in Cheyenne, Wyoming.
record.context: The former prospector’s later success shows that not everyone connected with the expedition met the same fate. His move into business also preserved a link between the earlier mountain search and life on the plains.

record.what: After enough pressure, the Colorado governor paroled Alfred in 1901.
record.context: The parole ended Alfred’s imprisonment before his death, though it did not erase the lasting importance of the case. It marked a significant change from confinement to conditional freedom after years of legal consequences.

record.what: Alfred died in 1907 at 65 years old.
record.context: Alfred’s death closed his personal role in a story that had continued for decades. His age places the end of his life well after the expedition and the legal controversy surrounding it.

record.what: In 1994, an 1862 Colt revolver was found at the site of the murders.
record.context: The weapon’s discovery returned physical evidence to the site long after the killings. It gave later investigators and historians a tangible object connected to the unresolved historical episode.

files.title: Packer's final account
files.body:
On March 11, a man calling himself John Schwartze came to the shop to buy supplies for a planned trip. The shop owner realized that the customer was actually Alfred Packer, and reported seeing Packer to the local sheriff. Packer was arrested and taken to Denver. General Adams later confirmed that the arrested man was Packer and took him away for trial. When Adams again asked what had happened, Packer gave a final story that he kept more or less until he died.

In Packer’s final story, the group left Chief Ouray’s camp with barely enough food for one grown man for one week. After two or three days, Packer said, they were hit by a brutal snowstorm. They kept trekking until they reached the base of a mountain and then a deep valley, where the snow was so deep they could barely walk. They climbed to higher ground, and by day four had only about a pint of flour left. For about the next ten days, Packer said, they lived only on rosebuds and pine gum while following a ridge to stay above the deep snow. Several of the men cried out at night and prayed to escape the mountains alive.

Packer said the party eventually crossed the main ridge and descended into a camp by a river. They followed the stream for a day until they reached a frozen lake, possibly Lake San Cristobal. They crossed the lake to reach some trees for shelter, and tensions among the men were rising. Shannon Bell became furious at Packer for getting them lost and at the others for acting pathetically. Shannon later told Packer to scout higher up the mountain for a way across. Packer took a pistol and went out alone, but found only steep slopes and more snow. On this scouting trip, he admitted for the first time to General Adams that he did not really know what he was doing and did not know that side of the mountains.

Packer said it took him all day to scout and return. When he came back, Shannon was sitting by the fire eating a piece of meat. Packer saw a man lying near the fire and the other three men lying around it without moving. Shannon rushed at him with a hatchet, and Packer shot Shannon in the stomach before finishing him after he fell. Packer said the night after Shannon’s death was the worst night of his life. In a later letter, Packer wrote that he was surrounded by “the midnight horrors of starvation” and “utter isolation.” He said he felt himself losing his sanity and beginning to understand Shannon’s condition because it was starting to happen to him too. In another letter, Packer wrote that “the greatest wonder was that I ever returned to a rational condition.”

Packer said that the next morning he tried to follow his tracks from the previous day but had to turn back because of snow and exhaustion. He built a small shelter from wood and branches, but it did not satisfy his hunger. He said the relief of eating overcame the horror of cannibalism, and he realized what he had to do to survive. Packer said he spent another two months in the shelter surviving off the rest of his party.

Sixty days later, Packer said, he saw an avalanche that left yellow clay behind, showing that he was in Slumgullion Pass. He recognized the area because Slumgullion Pass is known for its yellow color and was named after Slumgullion stew. In early spring, he finally knew where to go and set out up the mountain again. He wrapped some of the remaining meat for the journey and checked the other men’s pockets, where he found the money he later spent in Saguache. Packer said he had eaten his shoes, so he wrapped his feet in cloth and had to stop whenever his feet began to freeze. He would light a fire to warm his feet whenever that happened.

Near the agency, Packer said, he ate the last pieces of meat and may have dropped some that the Ute later found. He wanted to take them farther to show them the truth, but he also did not want to go back and be reminded of the horror. Packer said he escaped because he feared a mob would get past his guard and kill him. He had already nearly been killed by Preston Nutter and believed someone would eventually finish the job. After escaping, Packer said he went to Arkansas under a false name, worked on a ranch, then moved to Arizona and eventually to Cheyenne, where he was found.

After being imprisoned, Alfred wrote to anyone he could and claimed that the sentence was unjust. Alfred claimed that he had only killed Shannon and that the jury was full of biased and prejudiced people.

files.title: The agency investigation
files.body:
Two months later, only one man emerged from the mountains, and he looked oddly well fed instead of emaciated. When Alfred Packer arrived at the agency, he had rags over his feet, a long beard, a coffee pot hanging from one side, and a rifle on the other. General Charles Adams had Packer helped to a table with food, and Packer ate so quickly that he threw up. Packer said the others in his party had become too exhausted to continue, that he had suffered snow blindness and frostbite, and that he had been left behind to survive alone. He said that for months he had eaten rabbits, roots, and rosebuds, and that his experience as a guide had helped him survive. The video’s account says his appearance seemed strange because he claimed starvation while looking bloated and well fed.

Packer went to Saguache, where he spent over $100 on drinking and gambling and another $78 at a general store. The source says that the drinking and gambling spree would amount to about $3,800 in 2023 money. Packer often gave conflicting stories while drinking. Some people said he appeared to have a different wallet every time he went out, and he never seemed to run out of cash. He had sold his rifle at the agency for only $10, which did not explain his other money.

Preston Nutter was the leader of the other party that had stayed with the river and arrived at the agency in May. Preston went to Saguache to investigate and immediately suspected that Packer’s story was false. He told General Adams that the other men would not have left Packer for dead. Preston said the rifle Packer had sold belonged to an old man in the party and that Packer’s pipe belonged to Shannon Bell. He also pointed out that Packer had no money when he originally joined the party.

General Adams sent a mounted man to bring Packer in for questioning. When asked where he had got his money and how he had survived, Packer first said that his feet had become wet and cold and that he had stayed by the fire while the others went for food. Packer said he assumed the others had abandoned him when they did not return. A council was formed to investigate the matter, and two Ute men then arrived with pieces of flesh they said came from a human body found on a hill near the agency. Packer panicked, fainted, woke up, begged for mercy, and then gave a different account while sobbing. He reportedly said that it would not be the first time hungry people had been obliged to eat each other.

Packer’s confession said that ten days into the journey the group ran out of food. Packer said the oldest man died first, and the others ate him and took his rifle. Another man died five days later; the others ate him and found $133 in his pockets. Packer said Shannon Bell then shot the remaining men. He said he and Shannon carried some of the dead man’s flesh for food and covered up the rest. Packer said Shannon later tried to kill him too, and that he shot Shannon in self-defense after Shannon attacked him in a state of madness. General Adams had this confession written down and made Packer sign it as a sworn statement. Preston dragged Packer outside during the argument, and others had to intervene to stop Preston from killing him. Packer was arrested for manslaughter and imprisoned in a log cabin owned by the sheriff of Saguache.

files.title: The trials and sentence
files.body:
The video says Packer’s trial challenged many parts of his story, and that people believed the killings were deliberate and premeditated. The prosecution argued that Packer had intentionally led the men astray so he could steal their possessions by any means necessary, and it presented witness after witness to support that theory. Some of those witnesses had been members of the original party that left Utah. Preston Nutter testified that Packer was always trying to find out how much money the men had, while other witnesses described Packer’s behavior in Saguache and the conflicting stories he told about what had happened. When Packer took the stand, he spoke for six hours and admitted eating the other party members, but claimed that he had killed only Shannon and that Shannon was responsible for everything else. After the evidence was presented, the jury found Packer guilty of premeditated murder, theft, and several other charges, and Packer was sentenced to hang for his crimes.

The video also explains that the laws under which Packer was tried for murder had been created only after the crime had already happened. Before statehood, Colorado Territory did not have a statute under which Alfred could be tried for murder; Colorado became a state in 1876, and Colorado State established the specific laws for the crime only after the crime had taken place. Because of that legal problem—the lack of a murder statute at the time of the crime—Alfred’s conviction was overturned, and he had to be retried for manslaughter instead of murder. Alfred’s lawyers discovered this technicality before the hanging could happen, although the source describes both the original sentence as Packer’s sentence to hang and Alfred’s sentence to be hanged for his crimes.

In the new trial, Alfred again pleaded not guilty and repeated his story. The prosecution brought in hunters who said there was plenty of food in the area even in a bad winter. They testified that game such as rabbits and deer would have been easy to hunt, even for someone as inexperienced as Alfred, and argued that the cannibalism had to have been by choice because food would have been plentiful. The prosecution also argued that Alfred had at least led the group astray by hiking the more dangerous route in winter under the guise of being a guide; in the best-case scenario, it said, Alfred had been extremely negligent. Alfred was eventually found guilty of voluntary manslaughter and received 40 years in prison, described as the maximum of 8 years per man. At the time, the 40-year sentence was the longest prison sentence handed down in US history. Alfred was paroled by the Colorado governor in 1901, 18 years into his sentence.

files.title: The winter journey
files.body:
The trail from Utah to Colorado was covered in heavy snow, which slowed the wagons and made the route difficult to follow. The travelers used a compass for a while but still got lost, and by January they had completely run out of food. They began eating horse feed and even considered eating the horses. The men later described Alfred Packer as greedy, lazy, and constantly fighting with someone. On January 21, the starving party found a Ute camp in a valley just outside Montrose, led by Chief Ouray. Ouray gave them food, offered them shelter, and suggested that they stay with him until the weather improved. The party still had about 120 miles to travel and had to cross the San Juan Mountains. Ouray warned them that no Ute would attempt that crossing in those conditions and that doing so would mean certain death. The party nevertheless decided to split in two: half the men would remain with the horses and wagons until spring, while the other half would try to reach Los Piños Indian Agency. Ouray advised the travelers to drop down to the Gunnison River and follow it north to the agency, but Packer insisted that crossing the mountains directly would be better and much faster. Five of the men believed him and went with him.

The group without Packer followed the river and endured brutal winter conditions. They ran out of food before reaching the agency and would have starved if cowhands had not found them and taken them to a cattle camp. In April, the river group left the cattle camp, reached the agency in May, and discovered that Packer had already arrived and left alone. According to expedition leader Preston Nutter, Packer’s party followed the river on horseback until the horses could go no farther. Nutter then unloaded their supplies and walked the horses back to the Ute camp. He believed Packer’s party continued farther down the river and then took a trail high into the mountains. When Nutter turned back, Packer’s group had only about 14 days of food left. The men also lacked clothes adequate for warmth, had no snowshoes or flints, and had hardly any matches. Their only weapons and tools were a few rifles, one pistol, a hatchet, and some knives. No one heard from any of those men again until Packer appeared at the agency months later.

files.title: The bodies and the escape
files.body: In summer, General Adams took Packer and some men into the mountains to search for the bodies, but they found nothing. While Packer was waiting for trial in August, illustrator John Randolph traveled over the mountains near Lake City. Near a tributary of the Gunnison River, close to where Packer had said he left Shannon, Randolph saw something sticking out of the ground. He found five dead men in different states of decomposition. One body was nearly reduced to bones, apparently after animals had gotten to it. Two of the men had blunt-force injuries to the head, and another body, identified as Shannon Bell, had been stripped to the bones except for his hands and feet and also had a blunt head injury. The remains suggested deliberate removal of the edible parts; except for the first body, the damage did not look like animal scavenging. Randolph sketched the scene and reported it to authorities in Lake City. A volunteer team of 20 men later recovered the bodies. The coroner concluded that the men had been killed by blows to the head while asleep. None of the bodies had defensive wounds, and their skulls had similar markings. The men had rags under their feet, suggesting they may have eaten the leather from their shoes after running out of other food. A track to a makeshift shelter led investigators to suspect that Packer killed the men for their possessions, became stranded, and then ate them to survive. Packer’s charges were expected to be upgraded from manslaughter to first-degree murder, but someone gave him a key, a penknife, and some food, and he escaped from custody before the charges could be upgraded. Packer escaped from his cell and was not seen again for nine years.

files.title: Packer and the expedition
files.body: The man who emerged from the mountains was Alfred Packer, also known as the Colorado Cannibal. The original traveling party consisted of 20 men who did not initially know one another but all wanted to get rich. They were traveling to the newly found goldfields near Breckenridge, Colorado. Packer was not initially part of the party; the group met him about 25 miles south of Salt Lake City. He offered his services as a guide and claimed he knew the territory between Utah and “Brackenridge” well. Although the group thought he seemed odd, they agreed to take him with them because they believed someone who knew the way would be helpful. Packer actually had no idea where he was going. He had worked as a guide for only a few months, had a habit of getting lost and arguing with clients, and had a reputation for stealing and lying, so people who knew him generally did not like or trust him. As a younger man, Packer served twice in the Union Army during the Civil War and was honorably discharged both times because he had epilepsy and seizures. After his military service, he worked driving horses and other draft animals across the West. He also worked as a hunter, a range hand, and a laborer for mining companies, and he briefly tried mining in Colorado. He repeatedly lost jobs because of his bad attitude and because nobody trusted him. By the time the group reached the area just outside Montrose, Packer had gotten them that far largely by luck. After prison, Alfred worked at the Denver Post as a guard for a while. People described him as kind, modest, and even charitable, in contrast with his earlier reputation as grumpy, greedy, and untrustworthy. Alfred later moved to a city known as Littleton, where he bought a copper mine. There is a rumor that Alfred was a vegetarian when he died, but the narrator says that rumor should be taken with a grain of salt.

files.title: The release campaign
files.body: Alfred’s story eventually reached Polly Pry, a reporter for the Denver Post. After hearing it, Polly Pry partly believed him and used her position as a reporter to try to help him. She wrote stories about Alfred, portraying him as a man of the people. She claimed he was an ex-soldier persecuted by the establishment, in the wrong place at the wrong time, who had survived horrors most people could not imagine. She also claimed that his sentence was harsh because of the cannibalism, but that anyone would have done the same in that situation. # The full story behind a prospector's horrifying 1874 ordeal in Colorado's San Juan Mountains — what really happened, beyond what this video tells

1 sources · 5,100 raw words read · quotes verified 100% · confidence medium · 2026-08-30

## 1. The Read

Alfred Packer’s 1874 ordeal has two incompatible centers: a starving guide who says he found his companions dead and ate them to survive, and a known liar who may have led five men into the mountains, killed them, taken their money, and invented the cannibalism story afterward. The surviving evidence never cleanly resolves which version is true. The reconstruction and its uncertainties rest on a single narrated account, not independent confirmations. Packer had served briefly in the Union Army during the Civil War, but epilepsy and seizures led to two honorable discharges; later, his work as a guide, hunter, range hand, animal driver, miner, and mining-company laborer repeatedly ended because of his temper, dishonesty, or incompetence.

**Arrival and suspicion:** On April 16, 1874, Packer staggered into the Los Piños Indian Agency near Saguache during a fierce snowstorm, wearing rags instead of shoes, carrying a rifle and coffee pot, and begging for help. General Charles Adams’s men led him to a table. He was starving enough to vomit after eating too quickly, but he did not look like the nearly skeletal survivors agency workers were accustomed to seeing. His bloated face, full-looking belly, unexplained cash, and possession of other men’s belongings immediately made people suspicious of his first story. Packer said that the five men who had traveled with him became too exhausted to continue, and that snow blindness and frostbite had forced him to fend for himself. He said he survived for months on rabbits, roots, and rosebuds. In Saguache, he rented a room at a saloon, spent more than $100 on drinking and gambling—about $3,800 in 2023—and another $78 at a general store, despite joining the expedition with no money and receiving only $10 for the rifle he sold at the agency. People noticed that he gave conflicting accounts, seemed to have a different wallet whenever he went out, and never seemed to run out of cash. The journey from Utah to Colorado had quickly become dangerous, and the travelers eventually split over whether to continue.

**The expedition:** It began on November 20, 1873, when roughly twenty fortune-seekers left Bingham Canyon, Utah, for the newly advertised Colorado goldfields near Breckenridge, where newspapers claimed anyone with sense could make a fortune. Packer joined them about twenty-five miles south of Salt Lake City after claiming to know the route between Utah and Colorado. He had worked briefly as a guide, but his record was poor: he often got lost, argued with clients, stole from people, lied, and repeatedly lost jobs because no one trusted him. The first 260 miles were slow and difficult. Heavy snow obscured the trail, the wagons could barely follow a path, and the travelers eventually lost their way. By January, they had run out of food and were eating horse feed while considering whether they would have to eat the horses. On January 21, near Montrose, Chief Ouray and a Ute band found them, fed them, and offered shelter until spring. Ouray warned that no Ute would attempt the crossing in those conditions and said it would mean certain death. The prospectors ignored him because they feared that other prospectors would reach the goldfields first. The party split: some men stayed with the horses and wagons, while the group that included Packer and five others attempted to reach the agency.

**The route and the five missing men:** Starvation and exposure were plausible, but the same conditions make Packer’s decision to lead the group over the mountains look exceptionally reckless. Ouray advised the travelers to descend to the Gunnison River, follow it, and then turn north toward the agency. Packer insisted that crossing the mountains directly would be faster because he supposedly knew the country, and five men believed him. The alternative party followed the river, ran out of food, and would have starved without cowhands, who provided food and shelter at their cattle camp until spring. Its four members reached the agency in May, while Packer had arrived earlier, alone. The leader of Packer’s party later said that the men initially followed the river on horseback until the horses could go no farther, after which he unloaded their provisions and returned the animals to Ouray’s camp. They appear to have continued along the river before taking a high mountain route. Their leader knew they lacked enough supplies for a winter crossing but turned back after exhausting himself arguing with Packer. They had roughly fourteen days of food—barely enough for one man for a week—along with inadequate clothing, no snowshoes or flints, very few matches, a few rifles, a pistol, a hatchet, and knives. The leader’s decision to leave them was therefore itself a warning: he knew they could not reach the agency, but had had enough of Packer’s arguments. After that, no one heard from the five men again until Packer appeared at the agency.

**Changing stories:** Packer’s account became a public case involving survival cannibalism, although Preston Nutter, the river party’s leader, remained convinced that Packer had killed the men and stolen their possessions. Nutter challenged Packer’s first explanation, and Packer changed it. Nutter said the men would not have abandoned Packer, identified the rifle Packer had sold as belonging to an older party member, and recognized Packer’s discarded pipe as Shannon Bell’s. A council began questioning Packer. Two Ute men then arrived with pieces of flesh they said came from a human found on a nearby hill. Packer reportedly panicked, fainted, begged for mercy, and gave a sworn account. Before doing so, he said, “It would not be the first time that people had been obliged to eat each other when they were hungry,” making survival cannibalism part of the public case. He said the oldest man died ten days into the journey, after which the survivors ate him and took his rifle. Five days later, another man died, and they found $133 in his pockets. A third man died while Packer was away gathering wood, and the remaining men ate him. Packer said Bell then shot the others, carried some of the bodies as food, and buried the rest. Two weeks later, Bell allegedly attacked Packer, forcing Packer to shoot him in self-defense. Nutter did not believe the story; the dispute became so heated that he dragged Packer outside and nearly killed him before others intervened. Packer was arrested for manslaughter and held in the sheriff’s log cabin. When General Adams later took him and others into the mountains to recover the bodies, they found nothing and returned him to his cell.

**Bodies and forensic questions:** Illustrator John Randolph found the bodies in August near a tributary of the Gunnison, close to the place Packer had identified as Bell’s death site. Randolph saw five bodies in different stages of decomposition, several with blunt-force injuries to the head. One was nearly bones, apparently exposed to animals; Bell had been stripped almost to the bones, leaving only his hands and feet. The remains indicated that edible portions had been deliberately removed rather than simply consumed by animals. A team of twenty volunteers later retrieved the bodies. A coroner concluded that blows to the head had killed all five while they slept, citing the absence of defensive wounds and the similar markings on their skulls. Rags beneath their feet suggested that the men had eaten the leather from their shoes. A track led to a makeshift shelter, raising the possibility that Packer killed the men for their possessions, became trapped by worsening weather, and then ate them to survive. Hunters later testified that game remained plentiful in the area, including rabbits and deer, weakening Packer’s claim that cannibalism had been unavoidable. The findings were expected to upgrade his charge to first-degree murder. Before that happened, however, someone slipped him a key, penknife, and food. He escaped and remained under a false name for nine years.

**Packer’s final account:** After Cheyenne authorities recaptured Packer on March 11, 1883, he offered a final story that he largely maintained until his death. He had been using the name John Schwartze and was recognized by a former fellow prospector at a Cheyenne supply shop. Packer said the party had food for only one man for a week, that a snowstorm struck within two or three days, and that they survived for about ten days on rosebuds and pine gum while climbing ridges to avoid deeper snow. At a frozen lake, possibly Lake San Cristobal, Bell supposedly became furious and unstable. Packer went scouting with a pistol and returned to find Bell eating a piece of meat beside one dead man and three other apparently dead men. When Bell attacked him with a hatchet, Packer shot him in the stomach and then finished him. Packer spent roughly two months—about sixty days—in a shelter, finally ate Bell’s meat, and gathered more from the bodies. An avalanche exposed yellow clay that told him he was near Slumgullion Pass, whose color reminded settlers of slumgullion stew. He admitted taking money from the men’s pockets and later acknowledged that, during an earlier search expedition, he had deliberately stopped General Adams from reaching the bodies because he could not face the scene again. He said he escaped because he feared a mob would kill him after Nutter had nearly done so. He went first to Arkansas, worked on a ranch under a false name, moved to Arizona, and eventually reached Cheyenne.

**Trials and legacy:** The prosecution treated Packer’s survival account as a cover story for deliberate murder. Witnesses said he had tried to learn how much money the travelers possessed, knowingly led them onto the more dangerous winter route, and behaved dishonestly after reaching Saguache. Packer’s own six-hour testimony hurt him because he admitted eating the men but insisted that Bell alone was responsible for the killings. A jury convicted him of premeditated murder, theft, and other charges and sentenced him to hang. The court overturned that conviction because Colorado had not yet been a state when the killings occurred: Colorado Territory lacked a murder statute applicable to the crime, and the state laws used against him came later. At a second trial, the food-abundance argument and the charge of reckless guidance persuaded the jury. Packer was convicted of voluntary manslaughter and sentenced to forty years, the maximum eight years per victim and, according to the account, the longest prison sentence then imposed in the United States. Reporter Polly Pry of the Denver Post later recast him as a persecuted ex-soldier and argued that anyone would have eaten human flesh under those conditions. Her campaign produced petitions and helped secure his parole in 1901, after eighteen years in prison. Afterward, Packer worked briefly as a Denver Post guard, was described as kind and charitable, bought a copper mine in Littleton, and returned to prospecting. He died in 1907 at sixty-five; rumors that he had become a vegetarian remain unverified.

**What the evidence permits:** Later forensic examinations generally leaned toward guilt. One group reported marks across Bell’s forearms consistent with defensive injuries, contrary to Packer’s claim that Bell was shot once and quickly finished. But a 1994 discovery complicates that conclusion. An 1862 Colt revolver found at the murder site still held three .38-caliber bullets, and those bullets matched lead fragments found in Bell’s hip. That match suggests that at least part of Packer’s account may be true. The evidence supports parts of both positions: Packer may have been a deliberate killer, but parts of his desperate-survivor account may also be true. The fight remains between the deliberate-killer and desperate-survivor interpretations. What is honestly missing is a definitive reconstruction of who inflicted the head injuries, a fully documented chain of forensic analysis, and an independent account that can test Packer’s changing stories against the surviving evidence.

## 2. The Players

**Chief Ouray** — Ute camp leader near Montrose - sheltered the starving party and advised its route

On January 21, the starving party found Chief Ouray’s Ute camp in a valley just outside Montrose. He gave the men food, offered shelter, and warned that attempting the crossing in those conditions would mean certain death. He advised them to follow the Gunnison River north to the agency, but in Packer’s final story the group left his camp with barely enough food for one grown man for one week. One of the original prospectors who stayed with Ouray later opened a supply shop in Cheyenne, Wyoming.

**General Charles Adams** — Official who questioned Packer, recorded his confession, and took him to trial

General Adams had Packer brought to a table with food, then sent a mounted man to bring him in for questioning. He had Packer’s confession written down and signed as a sworn statement, and later took Packer and others into the mountains to search for the bodies, without finding them. Adams again questioned Packer, who gave a final story that he kept more or less until he died; Adams later confirmed Packer’s identity and took him away for trial.

**Preston Nutter** — Leader of the river party - challenged Packer’s account and identified the disputed belongings

Preston Nutter led the party that stayed with the river and reached the agency in May. He went to Saguache to investigate and immediately suspected Packer’s story was false, telling General Adams that the other men would not have left Packer for dead. Nutter identified the rifle Packer sold as belonging to an old man in the party and Packer’s pipe as Shannon Bell’s, and said Packer had no money when he joined. During an argument, Nutter dragged Packer outside and had to be stopped from killing him; he later testified that Packer was always trying to learn how much money the men had.

**Denver Post** — Newspaper connected to the arrest report and Alfred’s later prison-guard work

The local sheriff arrested Packer and took him to Denver after a man reported seeing him. Polly Pry was a reporter for the Denver Post. After prison, Alfred worked for a while as a guard at the Denver Post.

**Illustrator John Randolph** — Illustrator who found and reported the five bodies near Lake City

While Packer was awaiting trial in August, John Randolph traveled over the mountains near Lake City. Near a tributary of the Gunnison River, close to where Packer said he had left Shannon, Randolph saw something sticking out of the ground and found five dead men in different states of decomposition. He sketched the scene and reported it to authorities in Lake City.

**Gunnison River** — Route advised by Chief Ouray and followed by the parties toward the agency

Chief Ouray advised the travelers to descend to the Gunnison River and follow it north to the agency. The group without Packer stayed with the river, ran out of food, and would have starved if cowhands had not taken them to a cattle camp; they reached the agency in May. According to the expedition leader, Packer’s party followed the river on horseback until the horses could go no farther, then may have walked farther down it before taking a trail into the mountains. Randolph found the five bodies near one of its tributaries.

**Civil War** — Military context for Packer’s earlier service in the Union Army

As a younger man, Packer served twice in the Union Army during the Civil War. He was honorably discharged both times because he had epilepsy and seizures.

## 3. The Record

- **November 20, 1873** — The party that Packer eventually joined left Bingham Canyon, Utah, on November 20, 1873. (SRC_1)
  - This departure began the winter journey that would later become central to the Packer story. Leaving in late November placed the group in the mountains during a particularly difficult season.
- **1874** — In 1874, six men entered Colorado’s San Juan Mountains in winter hoping to reach newly discovered goldfields on the other side. (SRC_1)
  - The expedition was driven by the promise of gold, but its route required crossing the San Juan Mountains in winter. The decision put the men in a dangerous setting before they could reach the fields they sought.
- **April 16, 1874** — On the morning of April 16, 1874, workers at Los Piños Indian Agency near Saguache, Colorado were eating breakfast when Alfred Packer appeared in the mess hall doorway during a snowstorm. (SRC_1)
  - Packer’s unexpected arrival brought the mountain expedition into public view. Appearing at an agency during a snowstorm connected him to the missing prospectors and created the first immediate opportunity to learn what had happened.
- **1876** — Packer’s lawyers discovered that Colorado Territory had no murder statute before Colorado became a state in 1876. (SRC_1)
  - The legal discovery gave Packer’s defense a technical argument against a murder conviction. It also tied the case to Colorado’s changing legal status and the transition from territorial government to statehood.
- **1883** — In 1883, one of the original prospectors who had stayed with Chief Ouray opened a supply shop in Cheyenne, Wyoming. (SRC_1)
  - The former prospector’s later success shows that not everyone connected with the expedition met the same fate. His move into business also preserved a link between the earlier mountain search and life on the plains.
- **1901** — After enough pressure, the Colorado governor paroled Alfred in 1901. (SRC_1)
  - The parole ended Alfred’s imprisonment before his death, though it did not erase the lasting importance of the case. It marked a significant change from confinement to conditional freedom after years of legal consequences.
- **1907** — Alfred died in 1907 at 65 years old. (SRC_1)
  - Alfred’s death closed his personal role in a story that had continued for decades. His age places the end of his life well after the expedition and the legal controversy surrounding it.
- **1994** — In 1994, an 1862 Colt revolver was found at the site of the murders. (SRC_1)
  - The weapon’s discovery returned physical evidence to the site long after the killings. It gave later investigators and historians a tangible object connected to the unresolved historical episode.

## 4. The Files

### Packer's final account `single source`

On March 11, a man calling himself John Schwartze came to the shop to buy supplies for a planned trip. The shop owner realized that the customer was actually Alfred Packer, and reported seeing Packer to the local sheriff. Packer was arrested and taken to Denver. General Adams later confirmed that the arrested man was Packer and took him away for trial. When Adams again asked what had happened, Packer gave a final story that he kept more or less until he died.

In Packer’s final story, the group left Chief Ouray’s camp with barely enough food for one grown man for one week. After two or three days, Packer said, they were hit by a brutal snowstorm. They kept trekking until they reached the base of a mountain and then a deep valley, where the snow was so deep they could barely walk. They climbed to higher ground, and by day four had only about a pint of flour left. For about the next ten days, Packer said, they lived only on rosebuds and pine gum while following a ridge to stay above the deep snow. Several of the men cried out at night and prayed to escape the mountains alive.

Packer said the party eventually crossed the main ridge and descended into a camp by a river. They followed the stream for a day until they reached a frozen lake, possibly Lake San Cristobal. They crossed the lake to reach some trees for shelter, and tensions among the men were rising. Shannon Bell became furious at Packer for getting them lost and at the others for acting pathetically. Shannon later told Packer to scout higher up the mountain for a way across. Packer took a pistol and went out alone, but found only steep slopes and more snow. On this scouting trip, he admitted for the first time to General Adams that he did not really know what he was doing and did not know that side of the mountains.

Packer said it took him all day to scout and return. When he came back, Shannon was sitting by the fire eating a piece of meat. Packer saw a man lying near the fire and the other three men lying around it without moving. Shannon rushed at him with a hatchet, and Packer shot Shannon in the stomach before finishing him after he fell. Packer said the night after Shannon’s death was the worst night of his life. In a later letter, Packer wrote that he was surrounded by “the midnight horrors of starvation” and “utter isolation.” He said he felt himself losing his sanity and beginning to understand Shannon’s condition because it was starting to happen to him too. In another letter, Packer wrote that “the greatest wonder was that I ever returned to a rational condition.”

Packer said that the next morning he tried to follow his tracks from the previous day but had to turn back because of snow and exhaustion. He built a small shelter from wood and branches, but it did not satisfy his hunger. He said the relief of eating overcame the horror of cannibalism, and he realized what he had to do to survive. Packer said he spent another two months in the shelter surviving off the rest of his party.

Sixty days later, Packer said, he saw an avalanche that left yellow clay behind, showing that he was in Slumgullion Pass. He recognized the area because Slumgullion Pass is known for its yellow color and was named after Slumgullion stew. In early spring, he finally knew where to go and set out up the mountain again. He wrapped some of the remaining meat for the journey and checked the other men’s pockets, where he found the money he later spent in Saguache. Packer said he had eaten his shoes, so he wrapped his feet in cloth and had to stop whenever his feet began to freeze. He would light a fire to warm his feet whenever that happened.

Near the agency, Packer said, he ate the last pieces of meat and may have dropped some that the Ute later found. He wanted to take them farther to show them the truth, but he also did not want to go back and be reminded of the horror. Packer said he escaped because he feared a mob would get past his guard and kill him. He had already nearly been killed by Preston Nutter and believed someone would eventually finish the job. After escaping, Packer said he went to Arkansas under a false name, worked on a ranch, then moved to Arizona and eventually to Cheyenne, where he was found.

After being imprisoned, Alfred wrote to anyone he could and claimed that the sentence was unjust. Alfred claimed that he had only killed Shannon and that the jury was full of biased and prejudiced people.

(SRC_1)

### The agency investigation `single source`

Two months later, only one man emerged from the mountains, and he looked oddly well fed instead of emaciated. When Alfred Packer arrived at the agency, he had rags over his feet, a long beard, a coffee pot hanging from one side, and a rifle on the other. General Charles Adams had Packer helped to a table with food, and Packer ate so quickly that he threw up. Packer said the others in his party had become too exhausted to continue, that he had suffered snow blindness and frostbite, and that he had been left behind to survive alone. He said that for months he had eaten rabbits, roots, and rosebuds, and that his experience as a guide had helped him survive. The video’s account says his appearance seemed strange because he claimed starvation while looking bloated and well fed.

Packer went to Saguache, where he spent over $100 on drinking and gambling and another $78 at a general store. The source says that the drinking and gambling spree would amount to about $3,800 in 2023 money. Packer often gave conflicting stories while drinking. Some people said he appeared to have a different wallet every time he went out, and he never seemed to run out of cash. He had sold his rifle at the agency for only $10, which did not explain his other money.

Preston Nutter was the leader of the other party that had stayed with the river and arrived at the agency in May. Preston went to Saguache to investigate and immediately suspected that Packer’s story was false. He told General Adams that the other men would not have left Packer for dead. Preston said the rifle Packer had sold belonged to an old man in the party and that Packer’s pipe belonged to Shannon Bell. He also pointed out that Packer had no money when he originally joined the party.

General Adams sent a mounted man to bring Packer in for questioning. When asked where he had got his money and how he had survived, Packer first said that his feet had become wet and cold and that he had stayed by the fire while the others went for food. Packer said he assumed the others had abandoned him when they did not return. A council was formed to investigate the matter, and two Ute men then arrived with pieces of flesh they said came from a human body found on a hill near the agency. Packer panicked, fainted, woke up, begged for mercy, and then gave a different account while sobbing. He reportedly said that it would not be the first time hungry people had been obliged to eat each other.

Packer’s confession said that ten days into the journey the group ran out of food. Packer said the oldest man died first, and the others ate him and took his rifle. Another man died five days later; the others ate him and found $133 in his pockets. Packer said Shannon Bell then shot the remaining men. He said he and Shannon carried some of the dead man’s flesh for food and covered up the rest. Packer said Shannon later tried to kill him too, and that he shot Shannon in self-defense after Shannon attacked him in a state of madness. General Adams had this confession written down and made Packer sign it as a sworn statement. Preston dragged Packer outside during the argument, and others had to intervene to stop Preston from killing him. Packer was arrested for manslaughter and imprisoned in a log cabin owned by the sheriff of Saguache.

(SRC_1)

### The trials and sentence `single source`

The video says Packer’s trial challenged many parts of his story, and that people believed the killings were deliberate and premeditated. The prosecution argued that Packer had intentionally led the men astray so he could steal their possessions by any means necessary, and it presented witness after witness to support that theory. Some of those witnesses had been members of the original party that left Utah. Preston Nutter testified that Packer was always trying to find out how much money the men had, while other witnesses described Packer’s behavior in Saguache and the conflicting stories he told about what had happened. When Packer took the stand, he spoke for six hours and admitted eating the other party members, but claimed that he had killed only Shannon and that Shannon was responsible for everything else. After the evidence was presented, the jury found Packer guilty of premeditated murder, theft, and several other charges, and Packer was sentenced to hang for his crimes.

The video also explains that the laws under which Packer was tried for murder had been created only after the crime had already happened. Before statehood, Colorado Territory did not have a statute under which Alfred could be tried for murder; Colorado became a state in 1876, and Colorado State established the specific laws for the crime only after the crime had taken place. Because of that legal problem—the lack of a murder statute at the time of the crime—Alfred’s conviction was overturned, and he had to be retried for manslaughter instead of murder. Alfred’s lawyers discovered this technicality before the hanging could happen, although the source describes both the original sentence as Packer’s sentence to hang and Alfred’s sentence to be hanged for his crimes.

In the new trial, Alfred again pleaded not guilty and repeated his story. The prosecution brought in hunters who said there was plenty of food in the area even in a bad winter. They testified that game such as rabbits and deer would have been easy to hunt, even for someone as inexperienced as Alfred, and argued that the cannibalism had to have been by choice because food would have been plentiful. The prosecution also argued that Alfred had at least led the group astray by hiking the more dangerous route in winter under the guise of being a guide; in the best-case scenario, it said, Alfred had been extremely negligent. Alfred was eventually found guilty of voluntary manslaughter and received 40 years in prison, described as the maximum of 8 years per man. At the time, the 40-year sentence was the longest prison sentence handed down in US history. Alfred was paroled by the Colorado governor in 1901, 18 years into his sentence.

### The winter journey `single source`

The trail from Utah to Colorado was covered in heavy snow, which slowed the wagons and made the route difficult to follow. The travelers used a compass for a while but still got lost, and by January they had completely run out of food. They began eating horse feed and even considered eating the horses. The men later described Alfred Packer as greedy, lazy, and constantly fighting with someone. On January 21, the starving party found a Ute camp in a valley just outside Montrose, led by Chief Ouray. Ouray gave them food, offered them shelter, and suggested that they stay with him until the weather improved. The party still had about 120 miles to travel and had to cross the San Juan Mountains. Ouray warned them that no Ute would attempt that crossing in those conditions and that doing so would mean certain death. The party nevertheless decided to split in two: half the men would remain with the horses and wagons until spring, while the other half would try to reach Los Piños Indian Agency. Ouray advised the travelers to drop down to the Gunnison River and follow it north to the agency, but Packer insisted that crossing the mountains directly would be better and much faster. Five of the men believed him and went with him.

The group without Packer followed the river and endured brutal winter conditions. They ran out of food before reaching the agency and would have starved if cowhands had not found them and taken them to a cattle camp. In April, the river group left the cattle camp, reached the agency in May, and discovered that Packer had already arrived and left alone. According to expedition leader Preston Nutter, Packer’s party followed the river on horseback until the horses could go no farther. Nutter then unloaded their supplies and walked the horses back to the Ute camp. He believed Packer’s party continued farther down the river and then took a trail high into the mountains. When Nutter turned back, Packer’s group had only about 14 days of food left. The men also lacked clothes adequate for warmth, had no snowshoes or flints, and had hardly any matches. Their only weapons and tools were a few rifles, one pistol, a hatchet, and some knives. No one heard from any of those men again until Packer appeared at the agency months later.

### The bodies and the escape `single source`

In summer, General Adams took Packer and some men into the mountains to search for the bodies, but they found nothing. While Packer was waiting for trial in August, illustrator John Randolph traveled over the mountains near Lake City. Near a tributary of the Gunnison River, close to where Packer had said he left Shannon, Randolph saw something sticking out of the ground. He found five dead men in different states of decomposition. One body was nearly reduced to bones, apparently after animals had gotten to it. Two of the men had blunt-force injuries to the head, and another body, identified as Shannon Bell, had been stripped to the bones except for his hands and feet and also had a blunt head injury. The remains suggested deliberate removal of the edible parts; except for the first body, the damage did not look like animal scavenging. Randolph sketched the scene and reported it to authorities in Lake City. A volunteer team of 20 men later recovered the bodies. The coroner concluded that the men had been killed by blows to the head while asleep. None of the bodies had defensive wounds, and their skulls had similar markings. The men had rags under their feet, suggesting they may have eaten the leather from their shoes after running out of other food. A track to a makeshift shelter led investigators to suspect that Packer killed the men for their possessions, became stranded, and then ate them to survive. The man who emerged from the mountains was Alfred Packer, also known as the Colorado Cannibal. The original traveling party consisted of 20 men who did not initially know one another but all wanted to get rich. They were traveling to the newly found goldfields near Breckenridge, Colorado. Packer was not initially part of the party; the group met him about 25 miles south of Salt Lake City. He offered his services as a guide and claimed he knew the territory between Utah and “Brackenridge” well. Although the group thought he seemed odd, they agreed to take him with them because they believed someone who knew the way would be helpful. Packer actually had no idea where he was going. He had worked as a guide for only a few months, had a habit of getting lost and arguing with clients, and had a reputation for stealing and lying, so people who knew him generally did not like or trust him. As a younger man, Packer served twice in the Union Army during the Civil War and was honorably discharged both times because he had epilepsy and seizures. After his military service, he worked driving horses and other draft animals across the West. He also worked as a hunter, a range hand, and a laborer for mining companies, and he briefly tried mining in Colorado. He repeatedly lost jobs because of his bad attitude and because nobody trusted him. By the time the group reached the area just outside Montrose, Packer had gotten them that far largely by luck. After prison, Alfred worked at the Denver Post as a guard for a while. People described him as kind, modest, and even charitable, in contrast with his earlier reputation as grumpy, greedy, and untrustworthy. Alfred later moved to a city known as Littleton, where he bought a copper mine. There is a rumor that Alfred was a vegetarian when he died, but the narrator says that rumor should be taken with a grain of salt.

She claimed he was an ex-soldier persecuted by the establishment, in the wrong place at the wrong time, who had survived horrors most people could not imagine. She also claimed that his sentence was harsh because of the cannibalism, but that anyone would have done the same in that situation. Over time, Polly Pry’s stories made such an impact that local businesses began arranging petitions for Alfred’s release.

SECTION 1

The Read

Alfred Packer’s 1874 ordeal has two incompatible centers: a starving guide who says he found his companions dead and ate them to survive, and a known liar who may have led five men into the mountains, killed them, taken their money, and invented the cannibalism story afterward. The surviving evidence never cleanly resolves which version is true. The reconstruction and its uncertainties rest on a single narrated account, not independent confirmations. Packer had served briefly in the Union Army during the Civil War, but epilepsy and seizures led to two honorable discharges; later, his work as a guide, hunter, range hand, animal driver, miner, and mining-company laborer repeatedly ended because of his temper, dishonesty, or incompetence.

Arrival and suspicion: On April 16, 1874, Packer staggered into the Los Piños Indian Agency near Saguache during a fierce snowstorm, wearing rags instead of shoes, carrying a rifle and coffee pot, and begging for help. General Charles Adams’s men led him to a table. He was starving enough to vomit after eating too quickly, but he did not look like the nearly skeletal survivors agency workers were accustomed to seeing. His bloated face, full-looking belly, unexplained cash, and possession of other men’s belongings immediately made people suspicious of his first story. Packer said that the five men who had traveled with him became too exhausted to continue, and that snow blindness and frostbite had forced him to fend for himself. He said he survived for months on rabbits, roots, and rosebuds. In Saguache, he rented a room at a saloon, spent more than $100 on drinking and gambling—about $3,800 in 2023—and another $78 at a general store, despite joining the expedition with no money and receiving only $10 for the rifle he sold at the agency. People noticed that he gave conflicting accounts, seemed to have a different wallet whenever he went out, and never seemed to run out of cash. The journey from Utah to Colorado had quickly become dangerous, and the travelers eventually split over whether to continue.

The expedition: It began on November 20, 1873, when roughly twenty fortune-seekers left Bingham Canyon, Utah, for the newly advertised Colorado goldfields near Breckenridge, where newspapers claimed anyone with sense could make a fortune. Packer joined them about twenty-five miles south of Salt Lake City after claiming to know the route between Utah and Colorado. He had worked briefly as a guide, but his record was poor: he often got lost, argued with clients, stole from people, lied, and repeatedly lost jobs because no one trusted him. The first 260 miles were slow and difficult. Heavy snow obscured the trail, the wagons could barely follow a path, and the travelers eventually lost their way. By January, they had run out of food and were eating horse feed while considering whether they would have to eat the horses. On January 21, near Montrose, Chief Ouray and a Ute band found them, fed them, and offered shelter until spring. Ouray warned that no Ute would attempt the crossing in those conditions and said it would mean certain death. The prospectors ignored him because they feared that other prospectors would reach the goldfields first. The party split: some men stayed with the horses and wagons, while the group that included Packer and five others attempted to reach the agency.

The route and the five missing men: Starvation and exposure were plausible, but the same conditions make Packer’s decision to lead the group over the mountains look exceptionally reckless. Ouray advised the travelers to descend to the Gunnison River, follow it, and then turn north toward the agency. Packer insisted that crossing the mountains directly would be faster because he supposedly knew the country, and five men believed him. The alternative party followed the river, ran out of food, and would have starved without cowhands, who provided food and shelter at their cattle camp until spring. Its four members reached the agency in May, while Packer had arrived earlier, alone. The leader of Packer’s party later said that the men initially followed the river on horseback until the horses could go no farther, after which he unloaded their provisions and returned the animals to Ouray’s camp. They appear to have continued along the river before taking a high mountain route. Their leader knew they lacked enough supplies for a winter crossing but turned back after exhausting himself arguing with Packer. They had roughly fourteen days of food—barely enough for one man for a week—along with inadequate clothing, no snowshoes or flints, very few matches, a few rifles, a pistol, a hatchet, and knives. The leader’s decision to leave them was therefore itself a warning: he knew they could not reach the agency, but had had enough of Packer’s arguments. After that, no one heard from the five men again until Packer appeared at the agency.

Changing stories: Packer’s account became a public case involving survival cannibalism, although Preston Nutter, the river party’s leader, remained convinced that Packer had killed the men and stolen their possessions. Nutter challenged Packer’s first explanation, and Packer changed it. Nutter said the men would not have abandoned Packer, identified the rifle Packer had sold as belonging to an older party member, and recognized Packer’s discarded pipe as Shannon Bell’s. A council began questioning Packer. Two Ute men then arrived with pieces of flesh they said came from a human found on a nearby hill. Packer reportedly panicked, fainted, begged for mercy, and gave a sworn account. Before doing so, he said, “It would not be the first time that people had been obliged to eat each other when they were hungry,” making survival cannibalism part of the public case. He said the oldest man died ten days into the journey, after which the survivors ate him and took his rifle. Five days later, another man died, and they found $133 in his pockets. A third man died while Packer was away gathering wood, and the remaining men ate him. Packer said Bell then shot the others, carried some of the bodies as food, and buried the rest. Two weeks later, Bell allegedly attacked Packer, forcing Packer to shoot him in self-defense. Nutter did not believe the story; the dispute became so heated that he dragged Packer outside and nearly killed him before others intervened. Packer was arrested for manslaughter and held in the sheriff’s log cabin. When General Adams later took him and others into the mountains to recover the bodies, they found nothing and returned him to his cell.

Bodies and forensic questions: Illustrator John Randolph found the bodies in August near a tributary of the Gunnison, close to the place Packer had identified as Bell’s death site. Randolph saw five bodies in different stages of decomposition, several with blunt-force injuries to the head. One was nearly bones, apparently exposed to animals; Bell had been stripped almost to the bones, leaving only his hands and feet. The remains indicated that edible portions had been deliberately removed rather than simply consumed by animals. A team of twenty volunteers later retrieved the bodies. A coroner concluded that blows to the head had killed all five while they slept, citing the absence of defensive wounds and the similar markings on their skulls. Rags beneath their feet suggested that the men had eaten the leather from their shoes. A track led to a makeshift shelter, raising the possibility that Packer killed the men for their possessions, became trapped by worsening weather, and then ate them to survive. Hunters later testified that game remained plentiful in the area, including rabbits and deer, weakening Packer’s claim that cannibalism had been unavoidable. The findings were expected to upgrade his charge to first-degree murder. Before that happened, however, someone slipped him a key, penknife, and food. He escaped and remained under a false name for nine years.

Packer’s final account: After Cheyenne authorities recaptured Packer on March 11, 1883, he offered a final story that he largely maintained until his death. He had been using the name John Schwartze and was recognized by a former fellow prospector at a Cheyenne supply shop. Packer said the party had food for only one man for a week, that a snowstorm struck within two or three days, and that they survived for about ten days on rosebuds and pine gum while climbing ridges to avoid deeper snow. At a frozen lake, possibly Lake San Cristobal, Bell supposedly became furious and unstable. Packer went scouting with a pistol and returned to find Bell eating a piece of meat beside one dead man and three other apparently dead men. When Bell attacked him with a hatchet, Packer shot him in the stomach and then finished him. Packer spent roughly two months—about sixty days—in a shelter, finally ate Bell’s meat, and gathered more from the bodies. An avalanche exposed yellow clay that told him he was near Slumgullion Pass, whose color reminded settlers of slumgullion stew. He admitted taking money from the men’s pockets and later acknowledged that, during an earlier search expedition, he had deliberately stopped General Adams from reaching the bodies because he could not face the scene again. He said he escaped because he feared a mob would kill him after Nutter had nearly done so. He went first to Arkansas, worked on a ranch under a false name, moved to Arizona, and eventually reached Cheyenne.

Trials and legacy: The prosecution treated Packer’s survival account as a cover story for deliberate murder. Witnesses said he had tried to learn how much money the travelers possessed, knowingly led them onto the more dangerous winter route, and behaved dishonestly after reaching Saguache. Packer’s own six-hour testimony hurt him because he admitted eating the men but insisted that Bell alone was responsible for the killings. A jury convicted him of premeditated murder, theft, and other charges and sentenced him to hang. The court overturned that conviction because Colorado had not yet been a state when the killings occurred: Colorado Territory lacked a murder statute applicable to the crime, and the state laws used against him came later. At a second trial, the food-abundance argument and the charge of reckless guidance persuaded the jury. Packer was convicted of voluntary manslaughter and sentenced to forty years, the maximum eight years per victim and, according to the account, the longest prison sentence then imposed in the United States. Reporter Polly Pry of the Denver Post later recast him as a persecuted ex-soldier and argued that anyone would have eaten human flesh under those conditions. Her campaign produced petitions and helped secure his parole in 1901, after eighteen years in prison. Afterward, Packer worked briefly as a Denver Post guard, was described as kind and charitable, bought a copper mine in Littleton, and returned to prospecting. He died in 1907 at sixty-five; rumors that he had become a vegetarian remain unverified.

What the evidence permits: Later forensic examinations generally leaned toward guilt. One group reported marks across Bell’s forearms consistent with defensive injuries, contrary to Packer’s claim that Bell was shot once and quickly finished. But a 1994 discovery complicates that conclusion. An 1862 Colt revolver found at the murder site still held three .38-caliber bullets, and those bullets matched lead fragments found in Bell’s hip. That match suggests that at least part of Packer’s account may be true. The evidence supports parts of both positions: Packer may have been a deliberate killer, but parts of his desperate-survivor account may also be true. The fight remains between the deliberate-killer and desperate-survivor interpretations. What is honestly missing is a definitive reconstruction of who inflicted the head injuries, a fully documented chain of forensic analysis, and an independent account that can test Packer’s changing stories against the surviving evidence.
